content: A cigarette is a product designed for smoking, consisting of cured and finely cut tobacco leaves mixed with various additives. These are then rolled or packed into a paper-wrapped cylinder, typically less than 120 mm in length and 10 mm in diameter. One end of the cigarette is ignited, allowing it to smolder, while the smoke is inhaled through the opposite end, which is often filtered and placed in the mouth. Occasionally, cigarettes are smoked using a cigarette holder. While the term cigarette generally refers to tobacco-based products, it can also apply to similar devices containing other substances, such as cannabis. Colloquially, cigarettes are referred to as cigs, ciggies, smokes, stogies, squares, or fags. Cigarettes are highly addictive and are known to cause various health issues, including multiple types of cancer, cardiovascular diseases, respiratory conditions, circulatory disorders, and birth defects. Cigarettes differ from cigars in their smaller size, use of processed tobacco leaf, and white paper wrapping. In contrast, cigars are typically made entirely of whole tobacco leaves. Historically, the earliest forms of cigarettes were documented in Central America around the 9th century, where the Maya and Aztecs used reeds and smoking tubes to consume tobacco and other psychoactive substances during religious rituals. These practices were often depicted in pottery and temple engravings. Cigarettes and cigars were the predominant methods of smoking in regions such as the Caribbean, Mexico, and Central and South America until more recent times. Cigarettes were largely unknown in English-speaking countries until the Crimean War, during which British soldiers adopted the practice of rolling tobacco in paper, inspired by their Ottoman Turkish allies. The term cigarette emerged in the 18th century, originating from the practice of beggars in Seville collecting discarded cigar ends, wrapping the remaining tobacco in paper, and smoking them. This habit was depicted in 18th-century paintings by Francisco de Goya and later popularized in cultural works such as the opera Carmen by Georges Bizet. The popularity of cigarettes increased during and after the Crimean War, aided by the development of tobacco varieties suitable for cigarette production. Cigarettes were rationed to soldiers during World War I and World War II. By the latter half of the 20th century, the adverse health effects of smoking became widely recognized, leading to the introduction of text-based health warnings on cigarette packaging. While the United States has yet to adopt graphic warning labels, countries like Canada and Australia have implemented both textual and visual warnings to highlight the harmful effects of smoking. Modern cigarettes have evolved significantly since their inception. For example, the paper used in cigarettes often includes alternating sections of thin and thick material to optimize burning during inhalation and slow it when at rest. Synthetic particulate filters are used to remove some tar before it reaches the smoker. Commercially manufactured cigarettes are relatively simple in design, consisting of a tobacco blend, paper, polyvinyl acetate (PVA) glue to bond the paper, and often a cellulose acetate-based filter. However, significant attention is given to the creation of each component, particularly the tobacco blend, which may include over 100 ingredients. The paper used in cigarettes varies in porosity to regulate ventilation and burning rate. The tipping paper, which forms the mouthpiece, stabilizes the cigarette against saliva and moderates smoke delivery through laser-drilled air holes. The tobacco blend in cigarettes is carefully crafted to ensure consistent flavor, despite variations in tobacco crops due to environmental conditions. Modern cigarettes, especially those produced after the 1950s, incorporate a significant amount of tobacco processing by-products, such as leaf stems, tobacco dust, and small leaf pieces. These by-products are processed and reintegrated into the blend to maintain the cigarette's quality while improving production economics. Techniques such as expanding tobacco using supercritical carbon dioxide are employed to reduce tobacco density, allowing for the production of light cigarettes with less tobacco content. Flavoring agents, known as casings, are added to the tobacco blend to enhance taste and replace flavors lost during processing. These casings may include humectants like propylene glycol, flavoring products such as cocoa and licorice, and various sugars. A topping or fragrance is also added to ensure brand consistency in flavor and aroma. The final tobacco mixture is then filled into cigarette tubes and packaged. In recent years, manufacturers have sought to maximize profits by utilizing not only tobacco leaves but also plant stems, which are processed to resemble leaf material and blended into the cut tobacco. Before World War II, cigarette manufacturers often included collectible cards in their packaging, but this practice was discontinued during the war to conserve paper. In 1970, the Public Health Cigarette Smoking Act was signed into law in the United States, banning cigarette advertisements on television starting in 1971. Some tobacco companies attempted to circumvent this ban by marketing cigarettes as little cigars. Since 1998, the sale of cigarettes to individuals under 18 has been prohibited in all 50 U.S. states, with some states raising the minimum age to 19. Similar age restrictions exist in many other countries, with variations in enforcement and legal smoking age. Cigarette butts are the most littered item globally and are not biodegradable. The filters, made of cellulose acetate, take years to decompose and often end up in waterways, where they release toxic chemicals into the water supply. Tobacco advertising and sponsorship have been banned in many parts of the world, including the European Union, where the 2005 ban prompted changes in Formula One sponsorship practices. As of 2007, Ferrari was the only team retaining tobacco sponsorship, continuing its partnership with Marlboro until 2011.
